messages.subject: Re: MGCV estimation procedure of GMRF
parts:
I do not see the full picture here, but I am giving you my last guess.
Your code 
Q = -inla.graph2matrix(g) 
diag(Q) = 0 
diag(Q)=-rowSums(Q)  

gives a degenerate Q matrix: 1Q1=0, where 1=(1,1,1,...,1) vector.
This gives an intrinsic GMRF (see Rue and Held, 2005).

If your model runs fine without an intercept this is likely the problem.

Hans

messages.author: 02e03030784aa6a7
messages.subject: Re: MGCV estimation procedure of GMRF
parts:
Moving to from the Poisson to the normal is a correct move: when investigating these
unidentifiability issues, always simplify the model as much as possible.

A futher simplificaiton is to consider a diagonal Q from the start. After your manipulation
of Q, it will be completely zero, so x'Qx=0. You are then left with the gaussian -(Y-beta0-x)' I (Y-beta0-x) ,
which when integrated wrt x is 1 for all beta0, and this is why you get a zero gradient wrt beta0.

In general, the solution lies in the "intrinsic prior" literature (book by Rue and Held, 2005).

messages.author: e7cc390b005447b3
messages.subject: Re: MGCV estimation procedure of GMRF
parts:
I do not fully understand your solution,  Hans.

Here is my suggested solution: 

The likelihood of  a model with intercept is the same as the likelihood of a model without the intecept, since the x can absorb the intercept without changing the model. More formally:

(Y-beta0-x)I(y-beta0-x)=(y-tilde(x))I(Y-tilde(x)), and also tilde(x) Q tilde x =xQx. This holds for all beta0. The likelihood is therefore the same in both situations.

However, I have derived expressions for solutions for beta0 and for x where I set the gradient to zero (in the outer and inner problem, respectively). MGCV estimates an intercept and uses the same technique as TMB.  My expression for beta0 corresponds to the estimated value of beta0 in mgcv and the expression for x corresponds to the estimated values for x in TMB.
